steps.body: $1 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 7 = 21$, which is divisible by 3.

steps.title: Which digit can be left out
steps.body:
Using 4 distinct digits means omitting exactly one digit $d$. The digit sum is $21 - d$, divisible by 3 iff $d$ is divisible by 3: $d \in \{3, 6\}$.

- omit 3: $\{1, 4, 6, 7\}$, sum $18$ ✓
- omit 6: $\{1, 3, 4, 7\}$, sum $15$ ✓

steps.title: Arrange each set
steps.body:
No digit is 0, so every ordering of 4 distinct digits is a valid 4-digit number: $4! = 24$ per set.
$$2 \times 24 = 48$$

72 would need three valid sets; omitting 1, 4 or 7 leaves a sum not divisible by 3.

da-2024-da-1.approach: Recall the two standard facts: Poisson$(\lambda)$ has $E[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda$, and the standard normal $N(0, 1)$ is by definition the normal with mean 0 and variance 1.

steps.title: Statement (i): Poisson
steps.body:
For $P(X = k) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$:
$$E[X] = \lambda, \qquad E[X(X-1)] = \lambda^2$$
$$\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[X(X-1)] + E[X] - (E[X])^2 = \lambda^2 + \lambda - \lambda^2 = \lambda$$
Mean = variance = $\lambda$ → **true**.

steps.title: Statement (ii): standard normal
steps.body: $Z \sim N(0, 1)$ has density $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}$, mean $0$ and variance $1$ — that is the definition of *standard*. → **true**.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Both (i) and (ii) are true, which is option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: Both are standard facts: Poisson mean = variance = λ; N(0,1) has mean 0, variance 1.
(ii) is the definition of the standard normal, so it cannot be false.
(i) is true: $\operatorname{Var} = \lambda^2 + \lambda - \lambda^2 = \lambda$.
Both statements hold.

da-2024-da-1.shortcut: Poisson is the limit of Binomial$(n, p)$ with $np = \lambda$: variance $np(1-p) \to \lambda$ as $p \to 0$, equal to the mean.
pitfalls: Confusing "variance one" with "standard deviation one" — for $N(0,1)$ both equal 1 anyway.

da-2024-da-4.approach: In an undirected DFS every edge is either a **tree** edge or a **back** edge (no cross/forward edges), and an edge is classified by the direction in which it is *first* explored. Exploring $(u,v)$ from $u$ while $v$ is still undiscovered (white) makes it a tree edge — the case the official key intends.
concepts: Undirected graphs have no cross edges

steps.title: Edge types in an undirected DFS
steps.body: When DFS at $u$ examines $(u,v)$ for the first time, $v$ is either **white** (undiscovered) → the edge becomes a **tree** edge, or **gray** (an ancestor of $u$ still on the stack) → a **back** edge. $v$ cannot be black: a black $v$ would already have scanned $(v,u)$, so the edge would not be explored first from $u$. Hence undirected DFS has **no cross (or forward) edges**, and "gray" is a vertex colour, not an edge type.

steps.title: Typical case: v is still white
steps.body: $d[u] < d[v]$ means $v$ is farther from $s$ than $u$. In the natural run (adjacency of $s$ = $[u, a]$), DFS reaches $u$ first: $s \to u$, and $u$ scans $v$ while $v$ is still **white**, so $u \to v$ discovers $v$ and $(u,v)$ becomes a **tree** edge. This is the reasoning behind the official answer.

scene.caption: Order 1: s → u → v — (u, v) is a tree edge

steps.title: Eliminate the other options
steps.body: **cross**: impossible in an undirected DFS (step 1). **gray**: not an edge class at all. That leaves *tree* vs *back*; the key picks **tree** — option (A).

steps.title: Caveat: a back edge is also possible
steps.body: DFS depth is not BFS distance. Same graph, adjacency $s:[a,u]$, $v:[w,u,a]$, $w:[u,v]$, $u:[v,s]$: DFS goes $s \to a \to v \to w \to u$. At $u$ the first edge scanned is $(u,v)$, and $v$ is a **gray ancestor** of $u$ — so the edge is first explored $u \to v$ yet it is a **back** edge, although $d[u]=1<d[v]=2$. The question is therefore ambiguous; the official key (A) is kept and the record is flagged for review.

da-2024-da-5.approach: Second-derivative test: $f'(x^*)=0$ makes $x^*$ a stationary point and $f''(x^*)>0$ makes $f$ curve upward there, so $x^*$ is a **strict local minimum**. Nothing about the rest of the real line is known, so "global" cannot be claimed.

steps.title: Sign of the change
steps.body: Because $f''(x^*) > 0$, the term $\tfrac12 f''(x^*)h^2 > 0$ dominates $o(h^2)$ for all small $h \neq 0$, so $f(x^*+h) > f(x^*)$ in a neighbourhood of $x^*$: a **local minimum**.

steps.title: Why not global
steps.body: Counter-example: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$. Then $f'(1) = 3 - 3 = 0$ and $f''(1) = 6 > 0$, but $f(-3) = -27 + 9 = -18 < f(1) = -2$. So $x^*=1$ is a local but **not** a global minimum.

optionAnalysis.reason: $f'=0$ and $f''>0$ give $f(x^*+h) > f(x^*)$ for all small $h \ne 0$ — a strict local minimum.
Only local information is given; $f(x)=x^3-3x$ at $x^*=1$ satisfies the conditions but is not a global minimum. ("Necessarily" fails.)
A local maximum needs $f''(x^*) < 0$ — the opposite curvature.
Wrong curvature and wrong scope: a global maximum would need $f'' \le 0$ near $x^*$ at least.

da-2024-da-18.approach: Check each pair against the reason reconstruction can fail. Inorder + (pre or post) always works; preorder + postorder fails for general trees only because a node with a **single** child cannot be placed left or right — and a full binary tree has no such node. steps.body: The first preorder key is the root. Finding it in the inorder sequence splits the remaining keys into the left subtree (keys before it) and the right subtree (keys after it), and the sizes tell how to split the rest of the preorder. Recursing rebuilds **any** binary tree with distinct keys uniquely, so (A) is sufficient.

steps.title: (ii) Inorder + (iii) Postorder: unique
steps.body: Same argument with the root taken as the **last** postorder key: the inorder position of the root separates left and right subtrees, and recursion is forced. So (B) is sufficient.

steps.title: (i) Preorder + (iii) Postorder: unique for full trees
steps.body:
For a general binary tree, a node with one child gives the same pre- and postorder whether the child is left or right — that is the only ambiguity.

In a **full** binary tree each internal node has exactly two children. Then, after the root $r$, the next preorder key $\ell$ must be the root of the **left** subtree. In postorder, every key up to and including $\ell$ forms the left subtree; the keys after $\ell$ (before $r$) form the right subtree. Both pieces are again full trees, so recursion is forced. Hence (C) is sufficient.

steps.body: By independence $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{3-1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4-2} = \dfrac12\cdot\dfrac12 = \dfrac14$ on $[1,3]\times[2,4]$, so $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{area}(A)}{4}$.

steps.title: Region where $x \ge y$
steps.body:
Inside the square $y \ge 2$, so $x \ge y$ needs $x \ge 2$. For $x \in [2,3]$, $y$ runs from $2$ to $x$. That is the triangle with vertices $(2,2), (3,2), (3,3)$:

$$\text{area} = \int_2^3 (x-2)\,dx = \Big[\tfrac{(x-2)^2}{2}\Big]_2^3 = \tfrac12$$

da-2024-da-46.shortcut: $X \ge Y$ is possible only when both land in the overlap $[2,3]$: $P(X \ge 2)\,P(Y \le 3) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. Given that, both are i.i.d. $U[2,3]$, so $X \ge Y$ with probability $\tfrac12$. Total $\tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac18$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the joint density is $\tfrac14$, not 1 (answering 0.5).
Integrating over the whole $x$-range $[1,3]$ — for $x<2$ no $y$ in $[2,4]$ is $\le x$.
da-2024-da-46.verification: The shortcut (conditioning on both landing in $[2,3]$) gives the same $\tfrac18$; and $P(Y \ge X) = 1 - \tfrac18 = \tfrac78$ is plausible since $Y$ is shifted one unit up.

da-2024-da-47.approach: Use the standard exponential moments $E(X) = 1/\lambda$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 1/\lambda^2$ and solve the one equation.

steps.title: Mean
steps.body:
Using $\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-\lambda x}dx = \dfrac{n!}{\lambda^{n+1}}$:

$$E(X) = \lambda\cdot\frac{1!}{\lambda^2} = \frac1\lambda$$

steps.title: Variance
steps.body: $$E(X^2) = \lambda\cdot\frac{2!}{\lambda^3} = \frac{2}{\lambda^2}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - E(X)^2 = \frac{2}{\lambda^2} - \frac{1}{\lambda^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda^2}$$

steps.title: Solve $5E(X) = \mathrm{Var}(X)$
steps.body:
$$\frac{5}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\lambda^2} \;\Rightarrow\; 5\lambda^2 = \lambda \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda(5\lambda - 1) = 0$$

Since $\lambda > 0$, $\lambda = \dfrac15 = 0.2$.

da-2024-da-47.shortcut: For an exponential, $\mathrm{Var}/E = 1/\lambda$. Here the ratio is 5, so $\lambda = 1/5$.
pitfalls: Using $E(X) = \lambda$ (that is the Poisson mean) — gives $\lambda = 5$.
Using standard deviation $1/\lambda$ in place of variance.

da-2024-da-48.approach: Bayes' theorem: draw the two-level tree $T/\bar T$ then $S$, add the two $S$-leaves for $P(S)$, and take the share of the $T$-branch.

steps.title: Joint probabilities of the $S$-leaves
steps.body:
$P(T \cap S) = P(T)\,P(S\mid T) = 0.4 \times 0.3 = 0.12$

$P(\bar T \cap S) = P(\bar T)\,P(S\mid \bar T) = 0.6 \times 0.6 = 0.36$

da-2024-da-48.shortcut: Odds form: $\dfrac{P(T\mid S)}{P(\bar T\mid S)} = \dfrac{0.4}{0.6}\cdot\dfrac{0.3}{0.6} = \dfrac13$, so $P(T\mid S) = \dfrac{1}{1+3} = 0.25$.
pitfalls: Using $P(\bar T) = 0.6$ as $P(T)$.
Answering $P(S\mid T) = 0.3$ — the question asks for the reverse conditional.
Forgetting the $\bar T$ branch in $P(S)$.
da-2024-da-48.verification: $P(\bar T \mid S) = 0.36/0.48 = 0.75$ and $0.25 + 0.75 = 1$ ✓; the odds-form shortcut agrees.

da-2024-da-49.approach: The conditional density $f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x) = f(x,y)/f_X(x)$ is the slice $y \mapsto 2xy$ renormalised on $0<y<x$, so any constant factor (even a wrong one) cancels. Integrate the slice at $x = 1.5$.

steps.title: Check the density (why the key is MTA)
steps.body:
$$\int_0^2\!\int_0^x 2xy\,dy\,dx = \int_0^2 x\cdot x^2\,dx = \Big[\tfrac{x^4}{4}\Big]_0^2 = 4 \ne 1$$

So the given $f$ is **not** a valid joint pdf; the official key therefore awards marks to all (MTA).

steps.title: Conditional density at $X = 1.5$
steps.body:
Marginal (of the given function): $f_X(x) = \int_0^x 2xy\,dy = x\cdot x^2 = x^3$. Then

$$f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x) = \frac{2xy}{x^3} = \frac{2y}{x^2}, \quad 0<y<x$$

This integrates to $\frac{x^2}{x^2} = 1$ — the bad constant cancelled. At $x = 1.5$: $f(y\mid 1.5) = \dfrac{2y}{2.25}$ on $(0, 1.5)$.

steps.title: Expectation
steps.body:
$$E[Y\mid X=x] = \int_0^x y\cdot\frac{2y}{x^2}\,dy = \frac{2}{x^2}\cdot\frac{x^3}{3} = \frac{2x}{3}$$

$$E[Y\mid X=1.5] = \frac{2 \times 1.5}{3} = 1$$

answer.keyNote: The official key is "MTA" (marks to all) because the given $f$ integrates to 4, not 1. The conditional expectation is unaffected by the normalising constant, so the intended answer is 1.

da-2024-da-49.shortcut: Given $X=x$, $Y$ has density $\propto y$ on $(0,x)$ — a "ramp", whose mean is $\tfrac23$ of the way along: $\tfrac23 \times 1.5 = 1$.
pitfalls: Plugging $x=1.5$ into $f(x,y)$ without dividing by the marginal.
Using the range $0<y<2$ instead of $0<y<x$.
Trying to "fix" the pdf to $\tfrac12 xy$ and thinking the answer changes — it does not.
da-2024-da-49.verification: With the corrected pdf $\tfrac12 xy$: $f_X(x) = \tfrac14 x^3$ and $f(y\mid x) = \tfrac{xy/2}{x^3/4} = \tfrac{2y}{x^2}$ — identical, so $E = 1$ again.

da-2024-da-50.approach: Split the logarithm of the product into two logs and use the standard expansions $\ln(1+t) \approx t$ and $\cos x \approx 1 - x^2/2$.

steps.title: Split the log
steps.body: $$\frac{\ln\big((x^2+1)\cos x\big)}{x^2} = \frac{\ln(1+x^2)}{x^2} + \frac{\ln\cos x}{x^2}$$

steps.title: First term
steps.body: With $t = x^2 \to 0$: $\dfrac{\ln(1+t)}{t} \to 1$.

steps.title: Second term
steps.body:
$\cos x = 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4)$, so $\ln\cos x = \ln\Big(1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4)\Big) = -\dfrac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4)$, hence

$$\frac{\ln\cos x}{x^2} \to -\frac12$$

steps.title: Add
steps.body: $$\lim_{x\to0} = 1 + \left(-\frac12\right) = \frac12 = 0.5$$

da-2024-da-50.shortcut: Product inside the log: $(1+x^2)(1-\tfrac{x^2}{2}) \approx 1 + \tfrac{x^2}{2}$, and $\ln(1+\tfrac{x^2}{2}) \approx \tfrac{x^2}{2}$, so the ratio $\to \tfrac12$.
pitfalls: Treating $\ln\cos x \to 0$ and dropping it (answer 1).
Using $\cos x \approx 1 - x^2$ (missing the factor $\tfrac12$).
da-2024-da-50.verification: L'Hôpital: derivative of the numerator is $\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2} - \tan x$, of the denominator $2x$; the ratio $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2} - \dfrac{\tan x}{2x} \to 1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12$ ✓.

da-2024-da-51.approach: $M = uu^T$ has rank 1, so it has a single non-zero singular value. Since $M$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, singular values = eigenvalues, and the only non-zero eigenvalue is $u^Tu = \lVert u\rVert^2$.
concepts: Singular values of a PSD matrix

steps.title: Eigen-structure of $uu^T$
steps.body: $Mu = u(u^Tu) = \lVert u\rVert^2 u$, so $u$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lVert u\rVert^2$. Any $v \perp u$ gives $Mv = u(u^Tv) = 0$, so the other four eigenvalues are $0$.

steps.title: Singular values = eigenvalues here
steps.body: $M$ is symmetric and $x^TMx = (u^Tx)^2 \ge 0$, so $M$ is PSD; for such matrices $\sigma_i = \lvert\lambda_i\rvert = \lambda_i$. Hence the singular values are $\lVert u\rVert^2, 0, 0, 0, 0$.

da-2024-da-51.shortcut: For a PSD matrix, sum of singular values = trace. $\operatorname{tr}(uu^T) = u^Tu = 55$.
pitfalls: Answering $\lVert u\rVert = \sqrt{55} \approx 7.42$ — that is the singular value of the vector $u$, not of $uu^T$.
Expecting five non-zero singular values; $uu^T$ has rank 1.
da-2024-da-51.verification: Trace check: the diagonal of $uu^T$ is $u_i^2 = 1,4,9,16,25$, summing to $55$, which equals the sum of eigenvalues ($55+0+0+0+0$).

da-2024-da-52.approach: $\text{IG}(C,\text{Pitch}) = H(C) - \sum_v \frac{\lvert C_v\rvert}{\lvert C\rvert}H(C_v)$: count Green/Blue overall and within each pitch value, then apply binary entropy (base 2).
da-2024-da-52.shortcut: The $S$ branch has the same 3:2 mix as the parent (4:6 mirrored), so it contributes $\tfrac12 H(C)$; IG $= \tfrac12\big(H(0.4) - H(0.2)\big) = \tfrac12(0.971 - 0.722) = 0.1245$.
pitfalls: Using natural logs (gives $0.086$).
Forgetting to weight child entropies by $5/10$.
Miscounting the winners — Format is irrelevant to this split.
da-2024-da-52.verification: Shortcut gives the same $0.1245$; the key range $0.12$–$0.13$ contains it.

da-2024-da-53.approach: Sort the five training points by Euclidean distance from the diamond $(2,1)$ and take a majority vote among the $k$ nearest for $k = 1, 3, 5$ until squares win.

steps.title: $k = 1$: circle
steps.body: Nearest is $(1,1)$ at distance $1$ — a circle. Label: **circle**.

steps.title: $k = 3$: still circle
steps.body: Three nearest: $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(3,2)$ — both $\sqrt2$ points are included, so there is no tie problem. Votes: 2 circles, 1 square ⇒ **circle**.

steps.title: $k = 5$: square
steps.body: All five points vote: 2 circles, 3 squares ⇒ **square**. So the smallest odd $k$ is $5$.

scene.caption: k = 5: 3 squares vs 2 circles

da-2024-da-53.shortcut: There are only 2 circles and 3 squares, and both circles are among the 3 nearest. Squares can win only when $k$ reaches 5.
pitfalls: Mis-reading the diamond as $(2,2)$ or the circle at $(1,2)$ as a square.
Worrying about a tie at $\sqrt2$ for $k=3$ — both tied points are inside the top 3.
Answering 4 (an even $k$ is excluded by the question).
da-2024-da-53.verification: Even ignoring distances, squares need at least 3 of $k$ votes while both circles are within distance $\sqrt2$; for $k=3$ at most 1 square is in range, so $k=5$ is forced.

da-2024-da-54.approach: A Bayesian network factorises the joint as the product of each node given its parents: $P(U,V,W,Z) = P(U)\,P(V\mid U)\,P(W\mid U)\,P(Z\mid V,W)$. Read the four entries from the CPTs and multiply.
da-2024-da-54.shortcut: $W$ is a copy of $U$, so $P(W{=}1\mid U{=}1) = 1$; the other three factors are $0.5$ each: $0.5^3 = 0.125$.
pitfalls: Reading $P(Z=1\mid V=1, W=1)$ from the wrong row (rows $V{=}0,W{=}1$ and $V{=}1,W{=}0$ give 0).
Multiplying unconditional marginals instead of the CPT entries given the parents.
da-2024-da-54.verification: Sum over $Z$: $P(U{=}1,V{=}1,W{=}1) = 0.5\times0.5\times1 = 0.25$, and half of it has $Z=1$, giving $0.125$ ✓.

da-2024-da-55.approach: Use $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$. Since $X=1$ forces $Y=1$, $XY = X$, so $E[XY] = E[X]$.
da-2024-da-55.given:
| Outcome | $X$ | $Y$ | $XY$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| HH | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| HT | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| TH | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| TT | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Each outcome has probability $\tfrac14$.

steps.title: Means
steps.body: $E[X] = P(HH) = \tfrac14$; $\ E[Y] = P(\text{at least one H}) = 1 - P(TT) = 1 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac34$.

steps.title: Product moment
steps.body: $XY = 1$ only on HH, so $E[XY] = \tfrac14$.

steps.title: Covariance
steps.body: $$\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac14 - \frac14\cdot\frac34 = \frac{4}{16} - \frac{3}{16} = \frac1{16} = 0.0625$$

da-2024-da-55.shortcut: When $X \le Y$ are indicators with $X \Rightarrow Y$: $\mathrm{Cov} = E[X](1 - E[Y]) = \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac1{16}$.
pitfalls: Assuming $X$ and $Y$ independent (covariance 0) — they are built from the same tosses.
Taking $E[Y] = \tfrac12$ ("exactly one head") instead of $\tfrac34$.
